Script:


Timber Theft
24 November 2018

Voice
South Africa has roughly 1.3 million hectares of commercial timber plantations across the country, of which just over 80% is privately owned. The industry creates jobs for more than a 160 000 people and is one of South Africa’s largest export sectors, with exported timber products bringing in billions of rands of revenue each year. Unfortunately, its also a soft target for criminal syndicates. Richardsbay in Kwa-Zulu Natal is a major export hub for timber products in the country. And for the thieves, its timber Mecca.

Link Macfarlane
The timber that makes it’s way to Richardsbay is brought to mills like these, here it’s processed into pulp or it’s exported to international markets.

Voice
But according to our sources, a lot of the timber never makes it to the mills. Instead, sophisticated syndicates are skimming tons of timber from the truckloads arriving in Richardsbay every day. This hidden camera footage shows the thieves in action. And they’ve grown so brazen, they’ll do it in broad daylight.

Sound Up Khaifas Nzimande
There are people down there that are buying timber from our drivers, how they manage to get hold of them I don’t know.

Voice
Khaifas Nzimande has spent the last three decades in the timber industry. Having started as a humble labourer, he’s now a self made successful businessman, who not only owns his own trees, he also harvests for various growers, and owns a transport company which delivers the timber to Richardsbay.

Sound Up Khaifas
I serve as a harvesting contractor, and now I’m a transporter.

Voice
He recently fell victim to the Richardsbay syndicates, and says it hit his pockets hard.

Sound Up Khaifas
Your profit is very thin, so if something is stolen out of your load you basically get nothing. So you are working for your driver.

Sound Up Macfarlane
Every day hundreds of trucks arrive in Richardsbay, with tons of timber. However some of them don’t come straight to the mills, and that is where the theft begins.

Voice
The scam, which is called skimming, works like this. Once a farmer is ready to harvest, he’ll remove the trees on site and stockpile them. Hauliers will load the timber, on average about 34 tons per truckload, and transport them to the markets in Richardsbay. The syndicates will then contact the truck drivers and meet them at dumping sites like these found scattered around the mills.

Sound Up Mac
Well here’s another site that we’ve found timber lying all around, and about 2kms away from where the mills are. And as you can see this is exactly where the timber theft is actually happening.


Voice
At the dumping sites the syndicates will skim small amounts of timber from the load, just enough to stay under the radar. Gert Erasmus is the risk and security manager for large agri-cooperative TWK, who own a timber mill in Richardsbay. He’s hot on the heels of the timber thieves.

Sound Up Gert
I realised that their is a big problem with the theft of timber, and it’s a reality.

Voice
Erasmus spearheaded a joint investigation by the big five mills in Richardsbay in an attempt to put a stop to the theft. One of the skimming hotspots they identified was here, in an area called Alton, where trucks were dumping daily.

Sound Up Gert
Then it would throw off about two to three tons, and it’s only that amount of tonnage that will be thrown off, otherwise the transporter will see that the timber is being thrown off.

Voice
By skimming from enough trucks the syndicates can build up large stockpiles like these, and make millions from the sales.

Sound Up Gert
In our investigation, and like I said it was only for one month, there was 66 drivers that offloaded timber illegally at Alton.

Voice
The syndicates choose the sites carefully - they need to be close to the mills so that transporters won’t notice irregular fuel usage on the trucks, or see anything amiss on the tracking systems installed in the vehicles. Their activities are so prolific, they’ve even been inadvertently caught on Google Maps, as these images show. Once on site the syndicate members will pay the driver a small cash fee for the timber they skim from the load. One ton could be worth more than a R1000 at the mill, but the syndicate pays the driver much less.

Sound Up Khaifas
I understand per ton, they sell it roughly R200, R300.

Voice
Once the syndicates have enough stockpiled for a load, they’ll send in trucks to pick up the stolen timber, as seen in this footage. You need to be a registered supplier to sell to the mills, but the masterminds behind the syndicates have gotten around this either by working with, or starting their own legitimate companies that have all the paperwork in place to sell to the markets.

Sound Up Gert
That is where the problem comes. Because that is the persons that is creating the problem, that is creating the market, for the stolen timber to be delivered.

Voice
Farmer Brian Aitken, who’s recently sold his farm as part of a large land redistribution project, knows the financial impact of timber theft all too well.

Sound Up Brian
We lost in the order of R1.2 million worth of timber, a thousand tons of timber was lost over a four month period.



Voice
It’s not as easy as you might think to monitor your timber loads. You’d need a weigh bridge to weigh each load, and most people can’t afford their own. Stockpiles like this one on Aitken’s farm are often deep in heavily forested areas, miles away from public weigh bridges, in which the syndicates often also have staff on the payroll to doctor the paperwork.

Sound Up Aitken
It’s your medium sized grower who stands to lose the most, who doesn’t have their own equipment, doesn’t have their own weigh bridge, is dependant on service providers, so he has to go on the honesty of his service provider to tell him how many loads has been delivered on his behalf.

Voice
Khaifas Nzimande feels police should be doing more to eradicate the problem.

Sound Up Khaifas
I don’t want to say much, or to implicate them in any of this, but I don’t think they are doing enough.

Voice
Erasmus says the authorities could go along way in curbing the problem by simply enforcing the municipal by-laws.

Sound Up Gert
It’s illegal for timber to be discarded in municipal areas.

Sound Up Macfarlane
This is a municipal road, it’s a public road, and it happens in broad daylight. Why aren’t police then catching them?

Voice
Perhaps because of footage like this, which our sources say points to police involvement with the syndicates. In it, this police vehicle is seen driving into a large illegal timber dumping site near the mills. The cops arrive while this truck is being loaded with dumped timber, just meters away. The police talk to the man parked in this vehicle, who then points at the truck before making a phone call. The driver of the truck promptly arrives on the scene, speaks to the man in the vehicle and then approaches the police. We don’t know what is being said, but the driver soon walks back to his truck, apparently to go fetch something. He is then seen walking back to the police vehicle, where he allegedly pays a bribe to the cops. A few seconds later the police drive off, and the syndicates carry on with business as usual. We took our footage to the Richardsbay Police Station but the station commander was unable to see us, and their national communications office declined to comment. Erasmus says they’ve escalated the matter to the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigations, the Hawks. They believe they’ve identified the big boys behind the syndicates, who are able to deliver to the mills under the guise of being legitimate companies.

Sound Up Gert
Five persons, or suppliers, that had access to delivery notes, were responsible for those loads being delivered to the mills.

Voice
And he believes their cases are strong enough for the authorities to take action.

Sound Up Gert
So all the markets came together, and with the assistance of the NPA and the DPCI there was cases registered and the arrests will be imminent.


Voice
Whether the Hawks will swoop in to save the day remains to be seen. Ironically, while mills like TWK have taken the initiative to try and eradicate the problem, it’s not the markets that are losing money from the theft. It’s all the smaller role players along the supply chain that suffer the most.

Sound Up Brian Aitken
Timber is huge, it’s very important from a rural stability point of view. It creates wealth in the rural areas.

Voice
But everyone in the chain, from the grower who plants the trees, to the contractor who cuts and harvests them, to the transporter delivering the timber, gets paid for the weight of the final load delivered to the market.

Sound Up Brian Aitken
Everybody gets paid per ton.

Voice
So if the syndicate stole three tons from a single truckload, that’s three tons less that everyone downstream gets paid for, on each and every delivery. In Aitken’s case whole truckloads of timber were stolen by the syndicates, forcing him to go to extreme measures to monitor his product.

Sound Up Brian
I’ve gone to the expense of building a weigh bridge, trying to follow up on the whole process, from your contractor or service provider, right down to the haulier and to the markets.

Voice
But until the syndicates are stopped in their tracks, it will be people like Aitken and Nzimande, such critical role players in a key sector of our economy, who will have to carry the losses.

Sound Up Khaifas Nzimande
You’re working at a negative, because your profit will be at about three or four thousand, thats what you’re looking at. So now if they will take that R4000 or R5000 it means you must close down your business. Why must you continue?






















Promos

30 sec

Voice
We expose the brazen syndicates behind tons of timber theft happening in Richardsbay on a daily basis. And it’s costing South African farmers millions. (9 Sec)

Sound Up Brian
We lost in the order of R1.2 million worth of timber, a thousand tons of timber was lost over a four month period. (7sec)

Voice
While the looting continues on a grand scale, alleged police corruption is adding fuel to the fire. (6 sec)

Sound Up Khaifas
I don’t think they are doing enough (1:15 sec)

Voice
What will it take top stop the thieves in their tracks? (3 sec)

Sound Up Khaifas
it means you must close down your business. Why must you continue?





1 Promo 15 sec

Voice
We expose the inner workings of sophisticated timber theft syndicates operating in Richardsbay, and ask why police seem unable to stop the theft. (8sec)

Sound Up Brian
We lost in the order of R1.2 million worth of timber, a thousand tons of timber was lost over a four month period. (7sec)



2 Promo 15 sec

Voice
Tons of timber pilfered and alleged police corruption. An inside look into the problems faced by farmers trying to export their timber to the international markets. 9 sec

Sound Up Gert
there was 66 drivers that offloaded timber illegally at Alton.



Promo 10 sec
Hidden camera footage shows the wave of theft hitting timber growers hard - and exposes the alleged police corruption that’s fuelling losses of millions of rands.
